Hello, I’m Dr. Rivera, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’ll be spending a few quiet minutes with you today to see how your mood and emotions have been since your baby arrived.

We use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS**—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to help us pick up on signs of depression or anxiety that can sometimes show up after childbirth. It’s simply a way to check in, not to judge or label you, and everything you share stays between you and our care team.

I’ll ask you ten questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. For each one, just tell me what feels most true for you; there are no right or wrong answers. We’ll take it at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification at any time.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my partner makes a silly face or when the dog does something goofy, I catch myself giggling. It takes a little more effort, though; sometimes I have to remind myself to lighten up, but it’s definitely still there.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yes, I can still laugh—like when my little guy gives that big, gummy grin or when my husband tries to swaddle the baby and ends up tangled in the blanket himself. It might not come quite as automatically as it used to, but the funny side of things still reaches me most days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I still find myself looking forward to little things—like my morning coffee once the baby settles for his first nap, or our evening walk when my husband gets home. They’re small, but they feel good to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

I really don’t beat myself up much—if the baby spits up a ton or I’m a few minutes late with a bottle, I figure it’s just part of learning how to be a mom. I might think, “Oops, maybe next time I’ll try burping him sooner,” but I don’t keep replaying it or feel like I’m failing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do notice I get a little anxious sometimes, mostly about whether the baby’s breathing okay or if he’s eating enough. It’s not all the time, and it usually passes once I check on him, but every now and then I’ll catch myself worrying even when there’s nothing obviously wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I haven’t felt panicky or scared out of the blue—if I’m on edge, it’s usually because I’m worrying about the baby, not because a sudden rush of fear comes over me.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then it feels like a lot—yesterday, for instance, the baby wouldn’t settle, the laundry pile looked like a mountain, and I thought, “How am I going to get through the afternoon?” It passes once I check off one or two chores, but yeah, every so often it all stacks up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been all right. Once I’m out, I stay out—usually the baby’s wake-ups don’t even fully rouse me. I haven’t felt so down that it kept me tossing and turning.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt sad or miserable—tired, sure, and sometimes a little overwhelmed, but not down in the dumps. Most moments I still feel pretty steady.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried at all this week. Even when things feel hectic, I manage to keep it together—I might sigh or feel a little tense, but tears haven’t shown up.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You shared that, overall, you're settling into motherhood well-still able to laugh at your partner's antics and look forward to small pleasures like a quiet cup of coffee-while admitting that occasional worries about the baby and fleeting moments of being overwhelmed sometimes crop up. Your description paints a picture of normal postpartum adjustment rather than persistent low mood, and you clearly state you have not felt sad, had trouble sleeping, or experienced any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 5, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes situational worry about baby's well-being that still surfaces "for no good reason" between checks, fitting the frequency of "sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes periodic overwhelm ('every so often it all stacks up') and momentary inability to cope, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 5 falls well below the 8-point threshold suggesting probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse only two items above zero: mild, infant-focused worry (Q4=2) and periodic overwhelm when tasks pile up (Q6=2). These symptoms fall short of the five-or-more depressive criteria required by <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, and you explicitly deny anhedonia, persistent sad mood, guilt, sleep disturbance, tearfulness, or self-harm thoughts. No safety concerns are identified. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Continue routine paediatric and postpartum check-ups; re-screen with EPDS if mood changes
2. Practice brief stress-management techniques (deep breathing, 5-minute breaks) when feeling overwhelmed
3. Share childcare tasks with partner, family, or friends to ensure adequate rest
4. Contact your <med>primary care provider</med> promptly if low mood, anxiety, or hopelessness worsens or persists
5. Use local or online new-parent support groups for peer encouragement
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression Screening Summary (EPDS-based self-report)

Positive findings:
• Mild, situational anxiety focused on infant well-being (Q4) – worries resolve quickly after reassurance
• Episodic sense of being overwhelmed when multiple demands coincide (Q6) – mitigated by completing small tasks

Absence of significant symptoms:
• No anhedonia – maintains ability to laugh and anticipate daily pleasures (Q1, Q2)
• No excessive guilt or self-blame (Q3)
• No panic or unexplained fear (Q5)
• No mood-related insomnia (Q7)
• No persistent sadness, tearfulness, or crying spells (Q8, Q9)
• No self-harm ideation (Q10)

Clinical impression:
Screening does not indicate elevated risk for postpartum depression at this time. Mild, infant-centered anxiety and occasional feeling of being overwhelmed are within expected adjustment range; no safety concerns identified. Continue routine monitoring and psycho-education; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
